Country people, butchers, cattle drivers, street sellers, boys, thieves, loafers, and the lowest kinds of wanderers were packed together in one crowd. Drivers whistled, dogs barked, oxen bellowed and struggled, sheep bleated, and pigs grunted and squealed. Street sellers called out above the shouting, swearing, and arguments on every side. Bells rang and voices roared from every pub. Everywhere people crowded, pushed, drove animals, beat them, whooped, and yelled. The dreadful clash of noises rose from every corner of the market. Dirty, unwashed, unshaven figures kept rushing back and forth, plunging into the crowd and bursting out again. The whole scene was so loud and confusing that it overwhelmed the senses.

Mr. Sikes dragged Oliver behind him and pushed his way through the thickest part of the crowd. He paid little attention to the many sights and sounds that so amazed the boy. He nodded to two or three friends as they passed and turned down as many invitations to have a morning drink. He kept moving steadily until they had escaped the confusion and gone through Hosier Lane into Holborn.

“Now, youngster!” said Sikes, looking up at the clock on St. Andrew’s Church. “Nearly seven! You’ll have to hurry. Come on, don’t start falling behind already, Lazy-legs!”

As he spoke, Mr. Sikes gave his small companion’s wrist a sharp pull. Oliver quickened his steps into a trot, somewhere between a fast walk and a run, and kept up with the burglar’s long, quick strides as well as he could.

They went on at this speed until they had passed Hyde Park corner and were heading toward Kensington. Then Sikes slowed down, letting an empty cart that was some distance behind them catch up. When he saw “Hounslow” painted on it, he asked the driver, as politely as he could manage, to give them a ride as far as Isleworth.

“Jump up,” said the man. “Is that your boy?”

“Yes, he’s my boy,” Sikes answered, staring hard at Oliver and slipping his hand, as if without thinking, into the pocket that held the pistol.

“Your father walks a little too fast for you, doesn’t he, my lad?” asked the driver, noticing that Oliver was out of breath.

“Not at all,” Sikes cut in. “He’s used to it. Here, take my hand, Ned. Up you get!”

With these words he helped Oliver into the cart. The driver pointed to a pile of sacks and told the boy to lie down there and rest.

As they passed one milestone after another, Oliver wondered more and more where his companion was taking him. They passed Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, and Brentford. Still they travelled on as steadily as though their journey had only just begun.

He slipped out through the wooden panelling, an evil smile on his cruel, wrinkled lips, and the moon hid her face behind a cloud as he crept past the great projecting window, where his coat of arms and that of his murdered wife appeared in blue and gold. He glided onward like a wicked shadow; even the darkness seemed to recoil from him. Once, thinking he heard a call, he stopped. It was only a dog howling at the Red Farm, however, and he continued, muttering strange sixteenth-century curses and occasionally flourishing the rusty dagger in the midnight air. At last he reached the corner of the corridor leading to unfortunate Washington’s room. He paused there briefly, the wind tossing his long grey hair and twisting the unspeakable horror of the dead man’s shroud into bizarre, fantastic folds. Then the clock struck the quarter-hour, and he knew the moment had arrived. Chuckling to himself, he rounded the corner. Immediately he stumbled back with a pitiful cry of terror and buried his white face in his long, bony hands. Directly before him stood a dreadful apparition, as still as a carved statue and as monstrous as a madman’s dream! Its head was bald and polished, its face round, fat, and white; hideous laughter seemed to have twisted its features into a permanent grin. Scarlet beams streamed from its eyes, its mouth was a broad pit of fire, and a dreadful garment resembling his own wrapped the giant figure in silent, snowy whiteness. On its chest hung a sign bearing strange writing in old-fashioned characters: apparently some scroll of disgrace, some account of outrageous sins, some terrible chronicle of crime. In its right hand it held high a curved sword of gleaming steel.

Since he had never seen a ghost before, he was naturally terrified. After another quick look at the dreadful phantom, he fled to his room, stumbling over his long burial sheet as he raced down the corridor. Finally he dropped the rusty dagger into the Minister’s tall boots, where the butler discovered it in the morning. Safely inside his own room, he threw himself onto a small, narrow bed and covered his face with the bedclothes. After a while, however, the brave old Canterville spirit reasserted itself. He resolved to go and speak with the other ghost as soon as daylight came. Accordingly, just as the dawn began to silver the hills, he made his way back to the place where he had first seen the gruesome apparition. After all, he thought, two ghosts were better than one, and with the help of his new friend he might be able to take on the twins without danger.

I’m sure she would!”

The Widow Douglas’ magnificent hospitality offered an alluring bait. Together with Tom’s persuasions, it soon won the victory. They therefore agreed to tell nobody about their plans for the night. Before long Tom remembered that Huck might arrive that very evening and give the signal. This notion took much of the brightness out of his expectations. Yet he could not bear to forfeit the pleasure at Widow Douglas’. And why forfeit it, he argued—the signal had not come the previous night, so what made its arrival tonight any likelier? The evening’s certain enjoyment weighed more heavily than the doubtful treasure; and, like a boy, he resolved to follow the stronger temptation and forbid himself another thought of the money-box that day.

Three miles downstream from town the ferryboat halted at the entrance to a wooded hollow and made fast. The company poured ashore, and soon the distant woods and rugged heights rang on every side with cries and laughter. They tried every possible means of making themselves hot and weary, and presently the wanderers drifted back to camp equipped with formidable appetites. Then the assault upon the good things commenced. The feast was followed by a pleasant interval of repose and conversation beneath the wide-spreading oaks. At length someone called:

“Who’s coming to the cave?”

Everyone was coming. Bundles of candles were obtained, and immediately the whole company raced up the hill. The cave’s entrance lay on the hillside—an aperture in the shape of an A. Its heavy oak door was unbarred. Inside stood a little chamber, cold as an icehouse, whose natural walls of solid limestone glistened with chilly perspiration. There was romance and mystery in standing in that profound shadow and gazing out at the green valley bright with sunshine. But the grandeur of their surroundings soon ceased to impress them, and their frolicking resumed. No sooner was a candle lit than everyone charged its possessor; a tussle and a valiant defence ensued, but presently the candle was knocked over or puffed out, followed by delighted uproar and another pursuit. Everything, however, must end. Eventually the party filed down the steep slope of the main passage, their wavering line of flames faintly lighting the high rock walls almost to the place where they met sixty feet above. This principal passage measured no more than eight or ten feet across. At intervals of a few steps, other tall, even narrower fissures opened from it on both sides—for McDougal’s cave was simply an immense maze of winding corridors, running into one another and out again, and arriving nowhere.
